Calibration line of an assay

Source: R/tox.R
txcal.Rd

Fits the calibration line of a quantitative assay (the response, an analyte to internal standard peak-area ratio say, against the known concentration of each calibrator) by weighted least squares, and reads unknown samples off it. Weights 1/x^2 or 1/x keep the precise low calibrators from being swamped by the high ones, as is usual when the error grows with the concentration. The limits of detection and of quantitation follow the calibration-curve rule of ICH Q2: k[1] and k[2] (3.3 and 10) times the residual standard error over the slope.

Usage

txcal(conc, resp, w = "1/x^2", unk = NULL, k = c(3.3, 10))

Arguments

conc

The concentrations of the calibrators: positive numbers, at least three.

resp

The response of each calibrator: finite numbers.

w

The weights: "1/x^2", "1/x", "none", or positive numbers, one per calibrator.

unk

NULL, or the responses of unknown samples: numbers or NA.

k

The multipliers of the limits of detection and quantitation: two positive numbers.

Value

A list: fit, a named vector (int and slope of the line, r2 the weighted R squared, sigma the residual standard error on n - 2 degrees of freedom, lod and loq the limits); unk, NULL or a data frame with one row per unknown (resp, conc the concentration read off the line, flag: below_lod, below_loq or quantifiable); w, the weighting.

References

ICH (2023). ICH Harmonised Guideline Q2(R2): Validation of Analytical Procedures, final version adopted 1 November 2023, section 3.2.3.3. International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use. https://www.ich.org/page/quality-guidelines

Examples

conc <- c(5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250)
resp <- c(0.051, 0.098, 0.26, 0.49, 1.02, 2.47)
txcal(conc, resp, unk = c(0.03, 0.6))
#> $fit
#>          int        slope           r2        sigma          lod          loq 
#> 0.0005578058 0.0100118968 0.9990611257 0.0002794509 0.0921092214 0.2791188527 
#> 
#> $unk
#>   resp      conc         flag
#> 1 0.03  2.940721 quantifiable
#> 2 0.60 59.872990 quantifiable
#> 
#> $w
#> [1] "1/x^2"
#>
